introduction-testing-the-wetware.core: Resilience depends on people and processes as much as technology. Exercises test the 'wetware' (decisions, communication, runbooks, roles): live GameDays for technical response, tabletop exercises for scenarios you can't break for real.

first_principles.problem: Systems have perfect failover, but during a real incident nobody knows who decides, and the runbook is out of date.
truths: People respond the way they've practised.
Some scenarios can't be simulated live.
derivation: **GameDays**: inject real failures in a controlled way.

analogy.title: A fire drill
analogy.story: Sprinklers work, but if nobody knows the exits, people still get hurt.
analogy.breaks: Exercises disrupt work, so schedule and scope them sensibly.

example.title: What an exercise revealed
flow: Pager routed to someone on leave
No one knew who could approve failover
example.outcome: people and processes are as resilient as the systems.

check.a: Exercising the human side (decisions, communication, roles, runbooks), not just the technology.

gamedays-live-fire-exercises.core: A GameDay is a scheduled, controlled exercise where a team deliberately causes a real failure (killing instances, injecting latency, blocking a dependency) to practise detection and response and to validate resilience assumptions.

first_principles.problem: Teams believe their system tolerates an AZ loss but have never actually tried it.
truths: Control and safety limit the risk.
derivation: **Communicate** in advance (or run as a surprise for advanced teams).

analogy.title: A live-fire training exercise
analogy.story: Soldiers train with real equipment under controlled conditions, not just in classrooms.
analogy.breaks: Production GameDays need strong safeguards and stakeholder buy-in.

example.title: An AZ-failure GameDay
flow: Hypothesis: no user impact if AZ-a lost
Observe: alerts, LB shift, on-call actions

steps.label: Finding
steps.detail: A stateful service pinned to AZ-a gets a fix ticket.

check.q: Why define abort criteria for a GameDay?
check.a: To stop the exercise before real customer impact exceeds acceptable limits.

tabletop-exercises-ttx-the-executive-sim.core: Tabletop exercises walk participants (engineers, executives, legal, comms) through a scenario verbally, such as ransomware or a major breach. They test decisions, roles and communication without touching production.

first_principles.problem: You can't stage a real ransomware attack or region destruction, and executives have never practised crisis decisions.
truths: Some scenarios are too dangerous to simulate live.
Cross-functional gaps show up in discussion.
derivation: Write a **realistic scenario** with an evolving timeline.
A **facilitator** introduces injects and asks 'what do you do now?'

analogy.title: A flight simulator for executives
analogy.story: They practise the crisis without crashing the real plane.
analogy.breaks: Discussion can't reveal technical failures, so pair tabletops with GameDays.

example.title: A ransomware tabletop
flow: Inject 1: files encrypted on file servers
Inject 3: press calls asking for comment
Q: who decides on paying? who notifies regulators?

steps.label: Finding
steps.detail: No defined owner for the ransom decision, so a policy gets created.

check.q: When should you use a tabletop instead of a GameDay?
check.a: When the scenario can't be safely simulated live, such as ransomware or catastrophic data loss.

designing-the-injection.core: An injection is the scripted event that drives an exercise. Good injections are realistic, escalate over time, include ambiguous or misleading signals, and target specific capabilities you want to test.

first_principles.problem: Exercises with obvious, single-step scenarios teach nothing, because everyone knows the answer immediately.
derivation: Set **objectives**: what capability are we testing?
Make it **realistic**: plausible, based on real risks or past incidents.
Add **ambiguity and red herrings**; plan **facilitator controls**.

analogy.title: A good mystery novel's plot
analogy.story: Clues revealed gradually, some misleading, so the detective must reason rather than guess.
analogy.breaks: Over-complicated scenarios overwhelm people, so match difficulty to maturity.

example.title: An escalating injection script
flow: T+20: a batch job shows partial writes

steps.label: Tests
steps.detail: Detection, diagnosis, comms and legal escalation.

check.q: Why include red herrings in an exercise?
check.a: Real incidents contain misleading signals, and responders need practice reasoning through ambiguity.

after-the-exercise-findings-to-action.core: The debrief is the product. Capture what happened and what was expected, what went well, what gaps appeared (technical, process, people), and convert them into owned, tracked action items, then re-test.

first_principles.problem: Teams run an exciting exercise, note gaps on a whiteboard, and never fix them.

analogy.title: A sports team reviewing match footage
analogy.story: Watch the plays, identify the mistakes, drill the fixes, and test them in the next match.
analogy.breaks: Blame in debriefs kills candour, so keep them blameless.

example.title: Exercise findings → actions
flow: Gap: paging routed to old rota → fix rota sync (owner, date)
Gap: runbook missing failover step → update + test

check.q: What is the most important output of a resilience exercise?
check.a: Owned, tracked action items from the debrief, followed by re-testing.
